title: Groupoïdes de Teichmüller et les S0 Tg,!ν, S0 TG : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
This is a rewritten version of the previous page. The letter n is crossed out and replaced by m, and the 2n-gon is relabelled with m (= 2n written above). The page sets up the basic combinatorial object for the Teichmüller-groupoid notes.

Setup: let m ≥ 3 and let P be a regular m-gon in a real 2-dimensional vector space V. P is understood as centred at the origin, or as the affine image of a Euclidean regular polygon. Its vertex set Ĩ carries a structure of 'combinatorial polygon', which can be given equivalently as a cyclic order up to reversal, an adjacency 2-regular connected graph, or similar.

Claim: three groupoids are equivalent.
1. Combinatorial polygons with m vertices.
2. Pairs (V, regular m-gon in V).
3. Torsors under the dihedral group D_m = μ_m ⋊ Z/2. Here Z/2 acts on μ_m by ζ ↦ ζ^{-1}.

The reason is that each kind of object is locally (indeed globally) isomorphic to the standard model (V_0 = C, Ĩ_0 = μ_m = _mC^*). Its automorphism group is D_m: μ_m acts by multiplications z ↦ ζz and Z/2 by complex conjugation. The object is thus recovered as the twist Isom(standard, X), a D_m-torsor, and conversely.

The margin note says the exclusion of m = 2 is not strictly needed but the case is very degenerate ('two vertices!').

The next page continues:
- It defines D = Aut(V, Ĩ) and the set ω of the two orientations.
- It gives the exact sequence 1 → D^+ → D → Z/2 → 1 and the embedding of ω into D^+ as the two rotations by ±2π/m.
- It notes that m even is equivalent to the vertex set being stable under x ↦ −x.

The even case m = 2n is what serves the Teichmüller application. It is plausibly about the symmetric (antipodal) polygons relevant to discrete-symmetry or hyperelliptic-type strata in the Teichmüller tower. Here, though, it is only set up.
errors: For m = 2 the stated equivalence genuinely fails. A combinatorial 2-gon has automorphism group Z/2, while D_2 = μ_2 ⋊ Z/2 is the Klein four-group. Moreover, the linear automorphisms of (R^2, {±1}) form an infinite group, not a dihedral one. This is consistent with the margin remark that m = 2 is 'très dégénéré', but it is not merely degenerate: the three-way equivalence breaks.

'Regular polygon in a real vector space' without a Euclidean structure must mean an affine image of a regular polygon centred at 0. This is implicit and harmless, since any such polygon determines a unique invariant Euclidean structure up to scaling.

ideas.what: Combinatorial polygon structures on an m-element set are equivalent to D_m-torsors and to (real plane, regular m-gon), via the standard model (C, μ_m) with automorphism group μ_m ⋊ Z/2
ideas.modern_name: Classification of forms or twists by torsors under the automorphism group of a standard object; the dihedral group as Aut of a cyclic order up to reversal
ideas.where_published: The general 'objects locally isomorphic to a model ↔ torsors under Aut' principle pervades SGA 1, SGA 3 and Giraud. Dihedral/polygon combinatorics appear in Esquisse d'un programme in the discussion of cartographic objects and Teichmüller towers.

ideas.what: Exact sequence 1 → D^+ → D → Z/2 = Aut(orientations) → 1, with the orientations embedded in D^+ as the two generating rotations (next page)
ideas.modern_name: Orientation character of the dihedral group

deep.surprise_reason: This is a clean, canonical (torsor-theoretic) restatement of elementary facts about regular polygons and dihedral groups, rewritten from the previous page with notation changed from n to m = 2n. It is typical Grothendieck foundational care, but contains nothing new.
transcription_corrections: First line: 'n' is struck through and overwritten by 'm' ('Soient m un entier ≥ 3').
Second line: the polygon is 'à 2n côtés' with 'm=' written above, i.e. m = 2n.
Above 'forme un': the insertion is 'l'ens des sommets d'', giving the reading 'forme l'ens. des sommets d'un polygone combinatoire'.
(2): μ_m is defined as _mC^* (the m-torsion of C^*), written with 'def' over the equality sign.
(1): the product sign in D_m = μ_m · Z/2Z stands for a semi-direct product, with Z/2Z acting via ζ ↦ ζ^{-1}.
Diagonal margin, only partially legible: it says roughly that the exclusion of m = 2 is not necessary, but for m = 2 the situation is very degenerate (case of two vertices!).
